Schema: tools/website/README.md. check.py fails if version differs from VERSION, if released differs from CHANGELOG.md or the release tag, or if a removed command appears outside the removed list. Honesty rule: only what ships in the current release is stated as existing; everything else says planned or publishing soon.
is: dctx is an open-source (Apache-2.0) Rust context engine for AI-assisted coding: one local binary that packs a project into one structured block, or answers bounded, byte-stable symbol queries (find, read, neighbors, skeleton) as CLI output.
is_not: No RAG: no embeddings, no vector search, and the engine never calls a model.
No network: pack, map and cache make no network calls; the release check counts socket calls under strace and fails on any.
No agent loop: dctx answers one command at a time; the agent or the human decides what to ask next.

verify_download.available: Each release on GitHub ships prebuilt archives for Linux x64/ARM64, macOS x64/ARM64 and Windows x64 with a SHA256SUMS file.
verify_download.planned: Releases from 1.3.0 also ship keyless cosign signatures, CycloneDX SBOMs, build provenance and offline bundles; see [verification](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/blob/main/docs/VERIFYING.md).

modalities.name: CLI
modalities.line: `dctx pack PATH` for one structured block (clipboard, file or stdout); `dctx map find|read|neighbors|skeleton|...` for bounded symbol answers.

modalities.name: Task context
modalities.line: `dctx pack --for TEXT --budget N`: find, neighbors and read of the names in TEXT, cut to an estimated-token budget.

modalities.name: CI and prompt cache
modalities.line: Deterministic pack and map output; tree lines carry no timestamps by default, so the prefix stays stable across a touch.

scopes: System binary: the `dctx` on PATH belongs to you and your agents, and you upgrade it. Interactive agents call this one.

Project binary (Node from npm; Python and Go from CI): a binary installed by a project library lives inside that project (virtualenv, node_modules), pinned and managed by that package manager. Application code and CI call this one; a library never silently falls back to PATH.
Same engine, different owner. `dctx doctor` lists every binary in reach; verify each against SHA256SUMS and its cosign signature.
notice: dctx is an advanced tool with several ways to use it. Used well, it cuts irrelevant text from selected tool answers. It does not save tokens by default; savings depend on a system reusing byte-identical, prefix-stable context. Extra calls can add tokens. If you are new, follow the safe path: one project, the system binary, direct CLI commands. Measure before you change anything.

claims.text: 11 November 2026: 20 questions, a private 13-crate Rust workspace, claude-sonnet-5-5, dctx 1.3.0, three repeats per arm. Median total tokens [min, max]: grep plus reads 14,904,014 [14,604,149, 15,622,381]; dctx CLI (warm index) 14,157,974 [11,221,908, 15,613,375]. CLI median tokens were -5.01 % versus grep. On this corpus and model dctx did not save 25 % tokens; the pre-registered rule was not met. Official strict citation recall medians [min, max]: grep 10.10 % [10.10, 20.73]; CLI 14.46 % [8.36, 22.65]. Diagnostic file-level recall medians: 53.77 % and 71.70 %, respectively; diagnostic, not a replacement metric. The claim is accuracy and bounded context, not token savings. dctx on its own does not save tokens by default. Savings depend on a harness or agent system reusing byte-identical, prefix-stable context across long sessions; there is no measured, citable savings figure for such a system yet. One corpus, one model, no significance claim; corpus and raw answers private and cannot be published; dctx 1.3.0 is not current HEAD. Under ~200 files, use grep.
Byte stability: the same query on unchanged code returns the same bytes; 33 of 33 text and JSON answers were byte-identical after unrelated edits (Linux only).

The October and November in-house numbers (run 7: 140 of 140 task questions, cold index and warm latency) measure tool output only, as estimated stdout tokens and raw fact coverage without a model; they are not agent completion rates or session costs.
That a pack template changes model answer quality or cost is a hypothesis pending an A/B test; nothing on this site measures it.

notice_status: Receipts are planned. The safe path uses CLI commands from a shell or an agent's shell tool.
safe_path: Start with one project you know, not your whole disk.
Install the release archive from GitHub Releases and verify it against SHA256SUMS.
Run `dctx map find NAME`, then `dctx read ID`, from the project root.
Run the same task with grep plus file reads and with dctx; compare whole-session tokens and calls, not only answer size.

ways.name: CLI
ways.line: pack a project or one task into a bounded page for chat, scripts and shell agents.

ways.name: Agents, short session
ways.line: for a quick task grep plus a file read is often enough; add dctx only where a focused query saves turns.

ways.name: Agents, long session
ways.line: find, then read by stable id, with skeleton for orientation, in big files and long sessions.

ways.name: Libraries
ways.line: embed the engine in your own tool; the project pins its own binary and never re-implements engine logic.
ways.status: Rust from Git now; Python, Node and Go wrappers built in CI, Node on npm; Python and Go from CI

ways.name: CI and prompt cache
ways.line: byte-stable output keeps the prompt prefix the same between runs, so provider caches can hit.

personas.name: One giant folder
personas.gets: Short answers about only the part of the tree you name; the rest is never scanned.
personas.who: You work inside one very large tree, for example a 200 GB monorepo, data or document folder.
personas.modality: System binary, scoped roots, ignore rules at each root you query.
setup: Install the system binary from GitHub Releases and verify it against SHA256SUMS.
Write a `.dctxignore` at each root you will query: data, generated output and archives out (`.gitignore` is read too).
Decide which sub-roots a task can name: a package, a service, a document set.
Optional: set fail-fast ceilings with `DCTX_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES`, `DCTX_MAX_RECORDS` and `DCTX_MAX_ENTRIES`.
personas.expect: A bounded page that starts with a `# <place> find` header and lists one stable id per line. Only the named sub-root is scanned and indexed; `dctx cache status --json` shows what the cache holds, under a 2 GiB hard cap. A scan over a limit fails with an error instead of returning a partial index.
personas.pitfall: Pointing an agent at the whole root. Every call then has to scan or index far more than the task needs, and the cache cap can refuse it. Name the sub-root in the task, with `--place` or by starting in that folder.

personas.name: Many smaller projects
personas.gets: Install once, then run find and read from each project directory.
personas.who: You move between many small and medium repositories during the day.
personas.modality: System binary, called directly from a shell or an agent's shell tool.
setup: Install the system binary once and put it on PATH.
Run the dctx CLI directly from your agent's shell tool.
Start in the project directory, or use --place to name the project root.
Nothing else per project: dctx reads `.gitignore` and `.dctxignore` where they already are.
personas.expect: find returns stable ids; read returns the verified source bytes of one id. The captured run below shows find on the sample project.
personas.pitfall: Stale caches of projects you deleted or no longer use. Auto-clean runs once a day and drops unpinned roots after 30 idle days; to clean by hand, run `dctx cache status`, then `dctx cache gc --dry-run` or `dctx cache purge --root PATH --dry-run`.

personas.name: Agent builder embedding a library
personas.gets: Stable ids and the exact source bytes inside your own app, from the same engine as the CLI.
personas.who: You build an agent, editor or tool and want dctx inside it.
personas.modality: Project library with its own pinned binary. Install the Node wrapper with `npm install @tejl/dctx`; use CI artifacts for Python and Go, embed the Rust facade from a tagged Git dependency, or run a pinned CLI binary and read its `--json` output.
setup: Pin one version in your project, for example the Rust facade: `dctx = { git = "https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx", tag = "v1.3.1" }`.
Pass your own ignore rules: the library does not load `.gitignore` by itself; the host supplies selection policy, storage limits and the clock.
Move ids, not text: call `find`, keep the returned ids, call `read` with them.
personas.expect: The ten-line library example compiles and runs against an in-memory source. With the CLI, `--json` answers carry the same records, and `read` puts the exact source in `source_utf8`.
personas.pitfall: Re-implementing engine logic: parsing or slicing pack text, recounting budgets, rebuilding ids. Treat answers as opaque pages and stable ids; if you need a different shape, ask the engine for `--json`.

personas.name: Team or organisation admin
personas.gets: One verified, pinned version on every machine, with the same safety rules everywhere.
personas.who: You roll dctx out to a team or a fleet of machines.
personas.modality: System binary distributed through your own package channel, one pinned version everywhere.
setup: Download the release archives from GitHub Releases and verify them against SHA256SUMS and their cosign signatures; each release also ships an SBOM.
Ship one pinned version through your own package manager, image or configuration tool.
Ship shared ignore rules (`.dctxignore` and a global ignore); the built-in deny for secrets, `.git` and symlinks always applies.
Tighten the cache cap per machine if you need to: `dctx cache config --max-bytes N` can only lower it.
personas.expect: One line with the version on every machine; `dctx --version --verbose` adds the feature list and precision and cache limits. Every machine should print the same line.
personas.pitfall: Mixing project and system versions without checking. Run `dctx doctor` to list every binary in reach, and check `dctx --version` on PATH and the version each project pins, as part of onboarding.

install.system: Download the archive for your OS from GitHub Releases, verify it against SHA256SUMS, extract it and put `dctx` on PATH. Archives cover Linux x64/ARM64, macOS x64/ARM64 and Windows x64.
install.project: Install the Node wrapper with `npm install @tejl/dctx`, then run `npx @tejl/dctx`. It pins the matching `@tejl/dctx-<platform>` optional dependency. Use CI artifacts for Python and Go, or embed the Rust facade from a tagged Git dependency.

philosophy: The binary is everything. One file holds the engine and the CLI; there is no service to run, no account and no model behind it. It works offline and makes zero network calls. The same tree and the same question give the same bytes, so answers can be compared, cached and trusted.
